## What is the Yield Curve?

*Source: Stock Analysis Curriculum — Key Macro Indicators (Pages 3–4)*

The **yield curve** plots interest rates (yields) of US Treasury bonds across different maturities — from 3-month bills to 30-year bonds. It shows the relationship between time horizon and the rate the government must pay to borrow money.

**Three shapes and what they signal:**

| Shape | Description | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| **Normal** | Long-term yields > Short-term yields (10Y > 2Y) | Healthy economy, growth expected |
| **Flat** | Short and long yields nearly equal | Transition period, uncertainty |
| **Inverted** | Short-term yields > Long-term yields (10Y < 2Y) | **Recession warning** |

**Most watched spread:** 10-Year Treasury yield minus 2-Year Treasury yield (10Y–2Y spread)
- Positive spread = normal curve
- Negative spread = inverted = recession warning (highlighted in curriculum as key macro signal)

**Why the yield curve predicts recessions:**
An inverted curve means bond markets expect the Fed to cut rates in the future (due to a slowing economy). Historically, every major US recession since 1955 was preceded by an inverted yield curve, with a lag of 6–18 months.

**Why it affects stocks:**
- Normal curve → banks borrow short, lend long → profit → credit flows → bullish
- Inverted curve → banks' margins squeezed → lending tightens → credit crunch → bearish

## What Does an Inverted Yield Curve Mean?

*Source: Stock Analysis Curriculum — Key Macro Indicators (Page 3)*

An **inverted yield curve** occurs when short-term Treasury yields (2Y) exceed long-term yields (10Y) — the opposite of the normal relationship.

**The signal:** 10Y yield < 2Y yield → inversion → recession warning

**Why it happens:**
- The Fed has raised short-term rates aggressively (2Y tracks Fed Funds Rate closely)
- Bond markets expect the Fed will eventually need to CUT rates (because the economy will slow)
- Investors pile into long-term bonds for safety → long-term yields fall
- Result: short end elevated, long end suppressed → curve inverts

**What it means economically:**
1. **Banks stop lending** — they borrow at short-term rates and lend at long-term rates; when the curve inverts, their spread disappears → credit tightens → less investment
2. **Recession signal** — historically precedes every major US recession with a 6–18 month lag
3. **Market repositioning** — smart money starts rotating into defensives (XLP, XLU, XLV, GLD) before the recession officially hits

**What to do when the curve inverts (from curriculum):**
- Shift from "attack mode" to "defensive mode" 
- Reduce cyclical exposure (XLK, XLI, XLY)
- Increase defensive allocation (XLP, XLU, XLV, GLD)
- Watch for the curve to un-invert (re-steepen) — this often marks the actual recession beginning, not the inversion itself

## How Bond Yields Affect Stock Valuations

*Source: Stock Analysis Curriculum — Key Macro Indicators (Page 3), Fundamental Analysis (Page 9)*

Bond yields and stock valuations have an **inverse relationship** — when yields rise, stock valuations fall, and vice versa.

**Three mechanisms:**

**1. Discount rate effect (DCF / intrinsic value):**
Stock intrinsic value = PV of future cash flows discounted at risk-free rate + risk premium
When 10Y Treasury yield rises → discount rate rises → future cash flows worth less today → stock fair value falls

**2. P/E compression:**
From the curriculum: increasing interest rates directly contract P/E ratios. Higher yields mean investors demand more earnings per dollar of price → multiples compress

**3. Competition from bonds ("TINA" vs "TARA"):**
- Low yields: "There Is No Alternative" (TINA) → stocks are only game in town
- High yields: "There Are Reasonable Alternatives" (TARA) → bonds offer 4–5% risk-free → equities must offer more to compete → prices fall

**Which stocks are most sensitive:**
| Sensitivity | Stock Type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Highest | Growth/Tech (long duration) | Earnings are far in the future; higher discount hits hardest |
| High | REITs, Utilities | Valued like bonds; compete directly with yield |
| Lower | Value/Dividend stocks | Shorter earnings duration; less rate-sensitive |
| Benefits | Financials | Higher yields = wider lending margins |

**Rule:** When 10Y yield rises rapidly (>50bps in weeks), expect growth stock selloffs. When yields fall, growth stocks re-rate upward fastest.

## 10-Year Treasury Yield & Equity Markets

*Source: Stock Analysis Curriculum — Key Macro Indicators (Pages 3–4) + own knowledge*

The **10-year Treasury yield (10Y)** is the single most important interest rate in global finance — it is the benchmark for mortgages, corporate borrowing, and the discount rate used to value stocks.

**The core relationship:**

| 10Y Yield Movement | Equity Market Impact |
|---|---|
| Rising rapidly | Growth/tech selloff; P/E compression; sector rotation to defensives |
| Rising gradually (with strong GDP) | Acceptable; earnings growth offsets discount rate rise |
| Falling | Growth/tech rally; risk appetite returns; P/E expands |
| Very low (<2%) | "TINA" — stocks only game in town; valuations stretched |

**Key thresholds watched by the market:**
- **~4–5%** — the "competition zone" where bonds become a real alternative to equities for yield
- **Rapid >50bps moves** in weeks — triggers forced de-risking regardless of direction
- **10Y vs 2Y spread** — when inverted, signals credit tightening ahead (recession risk)

**Sector rotation driven by 10Y:**
- 10Y rising → short financials (XLF) — wait, financials BENEFIT from rising rates
- 10Y rising fast → avoid REITs, Utilities, growth tech
- 10Y falling → rotate into tech (XLK), REITs, growth

**Practical use:**
Track the 10Y daily alongside the S&P 500. When they both fall together → recession fear (risk-off). When stocks fall but 10Y also falls → rate cut expectations → often a buying opportunity for equities once sentiment stabilizes.
